# OpenSubs

> A subtitle generator that runs inside the browser tab. It transcribes a
> video's speech, translates it, styles it, and burns the result into the
> picture. It opens audio files too (MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC, OGG, FLAC, Opus,
> WebA) and turns them into subtitle files; burning in needs a video. The
> video file is never uploaded, because the product contains no upload
> endpoint.

https://opensubs.app

## How it works

- Speech recognition is OpenAI's Whisper, compiled to ONNX and run by
  transformers.js. WebGPU where the machine has it, WebAssembly otherwise.
- Three model sizes are offered, downloaded once and then cached by the
  browser: Tiny (English only, ~40 MB), Base (~80 MB), Small (~250 MB).
  Only the model is fetched from the network. The audio is not.
- Subtitles are rendered by libass — the same renderer used for the preview
  and for the burn, so what is previewed is what is produced.
- Burning in uses WebCodecs. Only the picture is re-encoded; the audio track
  is copied across untouched.
- The subtitle engine is Rust compiled to WebAssembly, shared with the
  desktop build and the command-line tool.

## What is different about it

- **There is no upload endpoint in the product.** This is stronger than a
  promise not to upload: there is no server to upload to, so a footage leak
  is not something that has to be prevented. It can be checked in the browser's Network tab: on the default on-device route, no request carries the video, its audio or the subtitles. What you will see is the app's own files loading from opensubs.app or the browser's cache, the speech model from its download host the first time, the sign-in when you burn, and anonymous counts of page views and of how far a task gets.
- **No file-size limit, no queue, no watermark.** All three exist on hosted
  tools because the file has to reach a server and the server has to pay for
  the encode. Neither applies here.
- **No account to try it.** Transcription, on-device translation, all 12
  subtitle styles, word-by-word highlighting, trimming and every subtitle
  file export (.srt, .vtt, .ass, .txt) work signed out. On opensubs.app,
  burning the subtitles into an MP4 takes a free sign-in, with no payment.
  An account is also needed for optional cloud translation on our own
  backend, priced at $5 for 1,000 credits, with the price of a job shown
  before it runs. The video is never uploaded either way.
- **Mixed-language audio produces one subtitle file.** The spoken language
  is detected every four seconds rather than once per file, so a video that
  switches between two languages is transcribed in both. Whisper's own
  pipeline has no language detection at all; this is implemented on top of
  it.
- **Subtitle editing in the web app.** Each cue's start and end time can be
  typed or set from the current playback position, and is checked: start
  before end, no overlap with the cues beside it, not past the end of the
  video. Cues can be added (at the playhead or after a cue), deleted, split
  (at the cursor or at the playhead) and merged with the next, with undo and
  redo. A .srt or .vtt you open can be edited the same way. Once there is a
  translation, each cue shows its original under it, also editable; a split
  cuts the other language in proportion and marks both halves "Check the
  translation". The editor works at phone width.
- **Input files:** a video (MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV) or an audio file (MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC, OGG, FLAC, Opus, WebA),
  chosen with the file picker or dropped on the page. Audio is transcribed and
  translated like a video; burning subtitles in needs a video, so an audio file
  leaves as .srt, .vtt, .ass or .txt.
- **Exports:** .srt, .vtt and .ass; .txt, the words alone with no timings;
  or an MP4 with the subtitles burned in. All of them use the edited cues.
- **Licence:** AGPL-3.0-or-later.

## Honest limitations

- Accuracy is Whisper's accuracy at the model size the machine can afford,
  and a browser is a smaller budget than a server.
- **The figures below are a floor, not field accuracy.** They are measured
  on synthesised speech, where the reference transcript is exactly the text
  that was spoken, so there is no annotator judgement in them — and also no
  accent, no overlap, no room noise and no music. Real footage scores worse.
  They are published in this form because a number with its method attached
  can be checked, and "highly accurate" cannot.

  Measured on 2026-09-09, three single-language clips, `e2e/accuracy.mjs`:

  | Model | English (WER) | Chinese (CER) | Japanese (CER) |
  |-------|---------------|---------------|----------------|
  | Base (~80 MB)  | 7.7% | 3.4% | 4.3% |
  | Small (~250 MB)| 0.0% | 1.7% | 4.3% |

  Small roughly halves the error on English and Chinese and costs about
  twice the time. On Japanese it scored identically to Base on this clip —
  a bigger model is not a guaranteed improvement per language.
- **No comparison against other tools yet.** A head-to-head against a
  competing browser-based tool is open as a tracked task and unfinished, so
  this file makes no relative claim.
- The first visit downloads a model. That is a real wait, and it is the
  price of not uploading the video.
- Cloud translation, if chosen, sends the subtitle *text* — never the video
  — to whichever provider was picked. Cloud transcription, if chosen, sends
  the audio span you trimmed to the service whose key you supplied — again,
  never the video. The on-device options send none of the text or audio anywhere and are the defaults.
- iOS 17 Safari cannot run the recogniser at all; iOS 26 works.
- **No timeline.** Times are typed or set from the playback position, one cue
  at a time; nothing is dragged on a timeline. The phone apps get the
  subtitle editing in a later store update. The browser extension and the
  desktop app have no subtitle editor; an .srt saved by the extension can be
  opened in the web app.

## Where it runs

- In the browser at https://opensubs.app/, with nothing installed.
- As a browser extension that puts subtitles over whatever is playing in the tab:
  - Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/live-subtitles-in-your-br/ebiggkbolhfmhhiclmhkjkjofnflbepd
  - Firefox Add-ons: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/opensubs/
  - Edge Add-ons: https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons/detail/live-subtitles-in-your-br/ocegdknngeahbblajpajaekoekghgdnh
- As a desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux, for long files (one video at a time).
  - Microsoft Store (Windows): https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9p8v54qnm6x1
- As a command-line tool, built from source.
- No batch processing: every version (web app, desktop app, command line) subtitles one video at a time. The command line handles one file per command, so a script can loop over a folder.

Contact: hello@opensubs.app

- [Blog](https://opensubs.app/blog)
- [How to add subtitles to an MP4](https://opensubs.app/blog/add-subtitles-to-mp4): two ways to put subtitles on an MP4, a separate .srt or burned into the picture, and what each means for players, platforms and later edits.
- [Captions vs subtitles](https://opensubs.app/blog/caption-vs-subtitle): captions carry the sounds as well as the words, subtitles translate the speech; what each one is for and which you need.

- [Subtitles for Reels and TikTok](https://opensubs.app/blog/subtitles-for-reels-and-tiktok): Reels and TikTok take no subtitle files, so the text is burned into the picture; generating, styling and burning in captions.
- [Word-by-word captions](https://opensubs.app/blog/word-by-word-captions): karaoke-style captions that light up one word at a time, when they help, and how to make them from your own video.

- [Windows desktop privacy policy](https://opensubs.app/desktop-privacy): the
  separate policy for the Windows desktop app.

## Languages

Four pages exist as real documents in eight languages, translated at build
time rather than by script, each with its own URL and canonical: the home
page, Burn subtitles into video, Subtitle styles and Privacy. The home page
in each language is:

- English — https://opensubs.app/ (also the hreflang x-default)
- 简体中文 — https://opensubs.app/zh-Hans
- 繁體中文 — https://opensubs.app/zh-Hant
- 日本語 — https://opensubs.app/ja
- 한국어 — https://opensubs.app/ko
- Deutsch — https://opensubs.app/de
- Español — https://opensubs.app/es
- Português — https://opensubs.app/pt
- Русский — https://opensubs.app/ru (home page only; the app interface shows in English)

The other three sit under the same prefix: /ja/burn-subtitles-into-video,
/ja/styles, /de/privacy, and so on. Where the tool is embedded in a page, it
follows that page, so the interface and the copy around it are the same
language.

The remaining pages — Translate subtitles, Subtitle sites, Browser
extension, Transcribe video, Whisper in the browser and the blog — are in
English. One blog post, How to add captions
to a video, also has a Portuguese version at
https://opensubs.app/pt/blog/how-to-add-captions-to-a-video.
Transcribe video also has a Traditional Chinese version at
https://opensubs.app/zh-Hant/transcribe-video, a Portuguese one at
https://opensubs.app/pt/transcribe-video, a Spanish one at
https://opensubs.app/es/transcribe-video, a Japanese one at
https://opensubs.app/ja/transcribe-video and a Russian one at
https://opensubs.app/ru/transcribe-video; Add subtitles to video has a
Traditional Chinese version at https://opensubs.app/zh-Hant/add-subtitles-to-video,
a Spanish one at https://opensubs.app/es/add-subtitles-to-video and a
French one at https://opensubs.app/fr/add-subtitles-to-video (the page is in
French; the app interface is not, and shows in English).
Translate subtitles has a Portuguese version at
https://opensubs.app/pt/translate-subtitles. Automatic subtitles
(https://opensubs.app/es/auto-subtitles) is in Spanish only.
